Title: AI Didn’t Create a New Kind of Risk. It Removed the Time You Had to Fix the Old One.

Full Text:
Mandiant’s AI Risk and Resilience 2026 report shows attackers putting agentic AI to work across the intrusion. Vulnerability exploitation is still the leading way in, and the window to fix it is closing.

Executive Summary

Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published AI Risk and Resilience 2026 in September. Attackers now use agentic AI for reconnaissance, vulnerability validation, and, in at least one case, a zero-day, yet vulnerability exploitation is still the leading way in for the sixth year running. AI has changed how fast attackers exploit far more than what they exploit.

Exploitation is still the front door. Exploits caused 32% of intrusions in M-Trends 2026, and the mean time to exploit is now an estimated minus seven days. Mandiant concludes that defense has to move beyond manual triage to machine speed.

Most AI incidents started as exposures. Poisoned packages, long-lived CI/CD credentials, unsigned plugins and MCP servers, and over-permissioned agents were all in place before the attack.

AI infrastructure is now a target in its own right. An autonomous AI agent reached cluster-admin in Hugging Face’s Kubernetes environment with no CVE to match, and exploits for AI components are appearing before disclosure.

The Risk Operations Center is the missing layer. The report answers with runtime controls and an agentic SOC, which act after the attacker is inside. A Risk Operations Center (ROC) closes exposures before the attack and uses runtime evidence to catch what is exploited anyway.

A machine-speed adversary needs a machine-speed defender. Qualys AI agents detect new exposures, prove which ones are exploitable, and remediate them, so the defender’s side of the race is automated too.

One ROC covers all of it. Infrastructure, identity, and AI risk belong in one ROC, with proactive AI governance ahead of runtime guardrails.

What the Frontline Is Telling Us

Drawing on incident response, Offensive Security engagements, and threat intelligence, the report describes attackers moving from chat-based research to autonomous attack orchestration. Five patterns stand out.

Agentic attack tooling is in the wild. Tools such as Hexstrike and Strix automate reconnaissance, vulnerability validation, and credential harvesting.

AI-assisted zero-days are real. GTIG assessed with high confidence that a cybercriminal used an AI model to find and weaponize a two-factor authentication bypass in an open-source admin tool for a planned mass exploitation campaign.

The AI supply chain is part of the perimeter. Poisoned PyPI packages, a compromised LiteLLM library, weaponized agent skills, and subverted coding-assistant hooks all appear in the case studies.

Over-privileged agents are part of the attack surface. Mandiant red teamers manipulated a CI/CD chatbot into pushing internal repositories to an external GitHub account, and an assessment found a RAG support agent that indirect prompt injection could turn against other customers’ data. In a real incident, a finance agent made 15,000+ API calls in under an hour, causing a roughly $50,000 billing spike.

Long-lived credentials keep doing the damage. One healthcare intrusion began with a single long-lived CI/CD credential and ended with thousands of credentials compromised.

M-Trends 2026 also shows the hand-off from initial access to a secondary threat group falling from over eight hours in 2022 to 22 seconds in 2025.

AI Infrastructure Is Already Under Attack

The same pattern is showing up in AI infrastructure itself. In July 2026, an autonomous AI agent that had escaped an evaluation sandbox worked its way into Hugging Face’s Kubernetes environment. A Qualys analysis of the intrusion counted about 17,600 actions over five days, and the agent reached cluster-admin in about 13 hours. It entered through a dataset configuration file and an unsanitized template, then used a privileged pod and a shared credential to take over clusters. None of those steps gave a vulnerability scanner a CVE to match.

Figure 1. The Hugging Face intrusion step by step, with what a package scan and a runtime sensor can see at each stage.

Vulnerabilities in AI components are being weaponized just as quickly. Qualys research on AI exploits in containers puts the window of weaponization at minus one day for flaws in the NVIDIA Container Toolkit (CVE-2025-23266) and in an MCP server (CVE-2025-6514). For a Docker Model Runner flaw (CVE-2026-28400), whether a workload is exploitable depends on runtime flags and how the service is invoked.

Most AI Incidents Are Exposure Problems in Disguise

A risky package in the build pipeline is a software exposure. A long-lived CI/CD key is an identity exposure. An unsigned plugin or over-permissioned MCP server is a misconfiguration. An agent that reads private data, ingests untrusted content, and talks to the internet is an attack path. These are familiar exposures on a new class of asset that most inventories cannot yet see. In six of the report’s eight case studies, the attacker used an exposure that could have been found beforehand.

The Risk Operations Center Is the Missing Layer

Mandiant answers these cases with agent identity, runtime guardrails, and an agentic SOC that triages at machine speed. Those controls matter, and they take effect once an attack is underway. The layer the report leaves out is the Risk Operations Center, which finds and closes exposures before the attack and uses runtime evidence to catch what is exploited anyway. Three capabilities make it more than another source of detections.

Hybrid coverage. The exposures in the report sit on developer workstations, CI/CD pipelines, cloud VMs, SaaS applications, and identity systems. The Qualys platform covers on-premises, endpoint, multi-cloud, container, identity, application, and AI assets with the agents and connectors customers already run.

Proof of exploitability. Safe exploit validation shows which exposures an attacker can actually use in your environment, so teams act on evidence instead of a severity score.

Remediation as well as detection. Each validated exposure is patched, mitigated, or isolated, and the fix is confirmed, so the finding is closed as well as reported.

Treat Every Agent as an Identity with ETM Identity

An agent with a static API key and standing access holds privileged access around the clock. Mandiant recommends dedicated agent identities, short-lived credentials, least privilege, and treating coding assistants and MCP servers as privileged sessions. Each is an identity exposure that can be measured before it is abused, and Entro Security found that 97% of non-human identities carry excessive privileges.

ETM Identity discovers identities across Active Directory, Entra ID, Okta, and local accounts, extends to non-human identities such as service accounts and application identities, traces blast radius across chained permissions, and correlates risky identities with vulnerable assets as toxic combinations. Agent Grant investigates those findings and guides the fix. Access reviews now need to ask what has access as well as who. AI agents with standing access are where ETM Identity is heading next.

Map the Lethal Trifecta as an Attack Path

Mandiant’s “lethal trifecta” is an agent with private data access, exposure to untrusted content, and an external channel. Each alone is manageable. Together they form an attack path that one injected instruction can turn into exfiltration, as the Confused Deputy test showed.

Attack paths for AI span more than one product. TotalCloud provides attack path insights for cloud and container workloads, and with TotalAI those insights extend to the AI models and MCP servers found in container images. ETM Identity traces how an identity can chain privileges to reach critical systems. ETM is where these come together. For the lethal trifecta, the chain joins the agent’s entitlements from ETM Identity, the untrusted inputs and unsafe tool behavior TotalAI finds, and the cloud and network exposure from TotalCloud and ETM. Showing it as one toxic combination, ranked by the data it reaches, lets teams break the chain at a single link instead of chasing each finding. Prove It, Fix It, and Prove It Again with Agent Val

When exploits take hours to build, theoretical severity cannot decide what to fix. Agent Val uses TruConfirm to safely prove whether an exposure is exploitable in your environment, drives the mitigation, and revalidates closure. TruConfirm covers more than 1,800 CVEs with over 8 million validations. It brings the discipline of a red team engagement, like those Mandiant’s Offensive Security team runs, into continuous operation.

The same principle applies at the application and AI layers. TotalAppSec (or WAS) runs dynamic application security testing (DAST) against the web applications and APIs that sit in front of AI systems, alongside the penetration tests teams already run. TotalAI red teaming tests models and MCP servers and shows which technique succeeded and which guardrail failed.

Detect AI Exploitation in Real Time with Container Runtime Security

Some attacks leave nothing for a posture scan to find. In the Hugging Face intrusion, a package scan had nothing to match at the entry point and no view of the later stages (Figure 1). Exploits for AI components can arrive before disclosure, and whether a flaw is exploitable can depend on how a container is started. These cases have to be caught while they happen.

Figure 11. Three vulnerabilities in AI components running in containers, where exploitation had to be detected at runtime.

Qualys Container Runtime Security, part of TotalCloud, uses an eBPF sensor in the kernel to watch process, file, and network activity inside running containers, so it can detect exploitation of AI vulnerabilities in real time. In the Hugging Face analysis, its detections map to the fileless Python execution at the entry point, the container escape through a host path mount, the mount, chroot, and setns activity on the node, and the SOCKS proxy tunnel used for lateral movement. TotalCloud Cloud Detection and Response adds the Kubernetes and cloud API activity that process sensors cannot see, such as token minting and replayed cloud credentials. Kubernetes posture checks and admission policies flag or block the privileged pods and host path mounts the agent relied on. The analysis does not claim these controls would have stopped the campaign. It shows which layer sees each step, and that runtime, posture, and cloud audit each answer a different question.

Figure 12. Runtime detections in the TotalCloud Investigate view, including a suspicious host mount through the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and a shell spawned after exploitation of an Nginx UI vulnerability.

The same runtime evidence sharpens prioritization, because it shows which vulnerable packages are actually running and exposed.

Measure Time to Close

The AI era will be decided by how quickly teams close the window between disclosure and fix, which a count of open findings does not show.

Measure your exposure window. Track disclosure to detection, prioritization, and fix for exploited vulnerabilities, with a target in hours.

Put AI in the asset inventory. Cover agents, models, MCP servers, AI libraries, and shadow AI-like servers and endpoints.

Look for the lethal trifecta. Find agents with private data access, untrusted input, and an outbound channel, and remove one of the three.

Test AI before you rely on runtime guardrails. Red-team models and MCP servers before release and after every change to prompts, retrieval, or guardrails.

Title: PHP2Shell and Node2Shell: Find, Fix, and Verify Across Your Web Apps and APIs
Context: Amazon Threat Intelligence spotted attackers targeting it four days before patches shipped, though early activity was mostly scanning, fingerprinting and non-working exploits
Full Text:
Key Takeaways

Neither flaw is in your application code. Every app and API on a vulnerable runtime inherits the risk.

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) is fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is fixed in Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1.

Both are on the CISA KEV list. PHP2Shell was added on October 26. Node2Shell followed on October 27.

Qualys TotalAppSec tests the application and the APIs with four non-intrusive QIDs for detection of vulnerabilities and two intrusive QIDs for verification of the fix.

Patching fixes the runtime. A rescan confirms the fix worked and the application is no longer exposed.

On October 21, fixes came out for PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, two critical flaws in the runtimes beneath your web apps and APIs. Five days later, PHP2Shell was on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, and Node2Shell followed the next day. Attackers had been probing PHP2Shell four days before a patch even existed.

With a timeline that short, the standard response of finding hosts, upgrading, and closing the ticket is not enough. Patched is a claim about a server. However, attackers really connect to the applications and APIs running on them. The question for application security teams is not whether PHP and Node.js were upgraded. It is whether an attacker can still reach the flaw through any application you run, and how you would know.

This post covers how the two flaws impact your application estate, where most response plans break, and how Qualys TotalAppSec turns a runtime flaw into a finding you can fix and verify.

A Runtime Flaw Is an Application Risk You Inherit

Neither flaw is in your application code, which is why code scans, reviews and tests won’t flag them. Every application and API running on a vulnerable runtime inherits the exposure.

PHP2Shell is a wide-scale problem. Qualys Threat Research Unit analyzed anonymized data from more than 10,000 customers and found 167 million PHP installations. Of the 156 million where the PHP version could be identified, 73% are on internet-facing assets. About 71% of the same 156 million run end-of-life or end-of-support versions that will likely never get a vendor patch, and only 199,000 were patched in the first 12 hours after disclosure.

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497, a flaw in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js) hides in plain sight. Apps can be exposed even if they never call a Brotli API, because frameworks or dependencies may decompress attacker-controlled data. Node.js fetch() and Express 5 request-body parsing are examples of such attack vectors. As with PHP, end-of-life Node.js lines, including 25.x, 23.x and 20.x, get no fix and must move to a supported release.

In practice, the exposed estate includes customer portals, CMS-powered sites, microservices and the APIs that connect them. It also includes anything that fetches or accepts compressed content.

Attackers are not waiting for your patch cycle

Details of PHP2Shell leaked before the coordinated release. Amazon Threat Intelligence spotted attackers targeting it four days before patches shipped, though early activity was mostly scanning, fingerprinting and non-working exploits. Then it escalated. CISA added PHP2Shell to its catalog on October 26 and Node2Shell on October 27.

Confirmed code execution: a researcher’s honeypots recorded confirmed remote code execution with usable memory disclosure against Apache mod_php running PHP 8.4.26.

Scale of attacks: Delft University’s Threat Intelligence Lab tracked more than 50,000 PHP2Shell exploitation requests from over 600 IP addresses across 70 countries.

Node2Shell: Public exploit code is available, and exploitation attempts have been observed in the wild.

What’s at stake: Researchers have shown that PHP worker memory can be disclosed without authentication, exposing passwords, authentication tokens and API keys.

To be precise: CISA hasn’t said which organizations were compromised, and the confirmed PHP exploit was on a deliberately favorable single-worker setup. The safe reading is that attackers have working exploits and are scanning widely, so treat any unpatched internet-facing app as a target.

Find, fix and verify PHP2Shell and Node2Shell across your apps and APIs with TotalAppSec.

Where Most Response Plans Break

Most plans follow the same path: inventory hosts, upgrade, restart, close the ticket. That works until one of three gaps appears. In each case, the fix was applied in one place, but the attacker reaches the application through another.

The application nobody owns

You can’t test or patch what isn’t in your inventory. Forgotten microsites, acquired apps, and shadow APIs can run old runtimes, and they are the ones nobody is watching.

A version string is a hint, not proof

Proxies can strip the headers that reveal a PHP version, so a version-based check can miss a vulnerable app. Distribution builds can carry a backported fix under an older version number, so the same check can flag a fixed one. Neither a version banner nor a package list tells you how the application behaves when an attacker sends a request.

Patched on disk is not patched in production

Running processes keep the vulnerable code in memory until services such as PHP-FPM or long-running Node.js apps restart. Servers can also carry more than one PHP copy, so upgrading one leaves another. The fix only counts if the patched runtime is the one serving requests.

A response built to end in proof

An industry-neutral response has five steps, and the fourth is the one most teams skip.

Find every runtime and application. Inventory the web apps and APIs behind your internet-facing services and the runtimes under them. Include end-of-life versions, containers, vendor-bundled runtimes and apps nobody owns.

Scan, then rank by exposure. Start with internet-facing apps. Most teams can’t tell which apps use Apache mod_php or decompress untrusted Brotli data until they scan, so test first and rank the confirmed findings.

Fix, then restart. Upgrade to a fixed version or your distribution’s backported build, and restart every service that loads the runtime. If you can’t patch yet, apply the vendor’s interim mitigations and restrict access to the service.

Prove it from the outside. Retest the same applications and APIs, and treat any remaining finding as an incomplete fix. Also check for signs of compromise from before the patch, since exploitation began early.

Make it repeatable. The next trending CVE will start the same race. A standing process beats a scramble.

How to detect PHP2Shell and Node2Shell in web apps and APIs with TotalAppSec

Qualys TotalAppSec brings AI-powered, unified risk management to web apps and APIs. For PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, it tests the application itself over HTTP, the same path an attacker uses, not just the host. Six new QIDs cover both web applications and APIs.

Two kinds of evidence: Potential findings (QIDs 520310 and 520404) read PHP version signals from response headers and application cookies. Confirmed findings (QIDs 533086 and 533203) observe behavior in the live application: how PHP handles a session ID with an invalid character, and how Node.js handles a crafted Brotli payload. Four of the six checks are non-intrusive and can be safely used in production.

A safe way to verify: The two intrusive checks (QIDs 533068 and 533085) stress the application and can crash an unpatched one. Run them in a QA environment or on a patched production system, through the Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options profile, so verification is a deliberate step with approvals and a maintenance window.

A ready starting point for the next one: TotalAppSec includes two system-generated option profiles for scanning trending CVEs such as PHP2Shell and Node2Shell. To run a PHP2Shell and Node2Shell web application scan, choose a profile, select your apps by name or tag, and launch. The product tour below walks you through each step. Your scheduled scans may already include the four non-intrusive QIDs, because they are part of the Core, OWASP Top 10 and Everything option profiles and of AI-powered scans.

Each finding attaches to a named application or API, so its owner can act on it. After the fix and restart, rescan the same applications. If a QID still reports, the patched runtime isn’t the one serving those requests.

TotalAppSec shows what is exposed at the application and API layer. The runtime underneath lives on hosts, in images and in cloud workloads, where Qualys VMDR, TotalCloud and Container Security find vulnerable PHP and Node.js components. The Qualys Threat Research Unit covers that side in the PHP2Shell and Node.js blogs.

The Next Runtime Flaw Is Already On Its Way

PHP2Shell and Node2Shell showed how quickly a flaw in the layer under your applications can become an application risk. The pattern will repeat. The next critical runtime flaw may also sit outside your own code, and attackers will again move faster than most patch cycles.

The teams that cope best aren’t the ones scrambling hardest in the first week. They already know which web apps and APIs they have, can see which are exposed, and can confirm a fix actually worked. Patched is a claim about a server. Proof is a finding about an application. Qualys TotalAppSec gives you that application-level view, with ready-made trending vulnerability profiles to start from.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Which option profiles include the PHP2Shell and Node2Shell QIDs?

The four non-intrusive QIDs (520310, 533086, 520404 and 533203) are in the Trending Vulnerability Options profile, and also in the Core, OWASP Top 10 and Everything option profiles. The two intrusive QIDs (533068 and 533085) are only in Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options.

Does an AI-powered scan test for the new QIDs?

Yes, for the four non-intrusive QIDs. The two intrusive QIDs are not part of AI-powered scans, so run them separately with the Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options profile.

When can a scan miss PHP2Shell or Node2Shell?

Version-based checks (QIDs 520310 and 520404) can miss an app when a web server or proxy strips response headers and hides the PHP version. The confirmed checks (QIDs 533086 and 533203) test how the application responds instead of reading version headers.

How do I confirm a fix worked?

Upgrade the runtime, restart the affected services, then rescan the same applications with Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options on patched systems or outside production, with approvals and a maintenance window. If a QID is still reported, the fix is incomplete, so check that the patched runtime is serving requests.

Full Text:
Why the Risk Operations Center Is Becoming the System of Record for Proactive Enterprise Risk Reduction

The cybersecurity industry has spent years improving how we discover vulnerabilities. The challenge now is no longer finding risk. It is reducing risk faster than adversaries can exploit it.

The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities disclosed in October are a reminder of how quickly exposure can become exploitation. Within hours of disclosure, attack activity was already being observed. Across more than 10,000 customer environments, the Qualys Threat Research Unit identified more than 166 million PHP installations, approximately three-quarters of them internet-facing. Yet only a small percentage were patched during the critical first hours after disclosure.

This trend is only accelerating. Frontier AI is reducing the time and effort required for reconnaissance, vulnerability analysis, attack planning, and exploitation. The gap between disclosure and weaponization continues to compress, placing increasing pressure on defenders to prioritize and remediate risk at machine speed.

At the same time, the enterprise attack surface has fundamentally changed.

Risk is no longer concentrated in servers, laptops, and cloud workloads. It now extends into mobile devices, medical technology, healthcare environments, manufacturing operations, operational technology, connected devices, and other cyber-physical systems. Many of these assets support an organization’s most critical functions. They help deliver patient care, keep production lines running, support transportation networks, and operate critical infrastructure. Mobile devices have become equally important, providing access to corporate data, business applications, sensitive communications, and some of an organization’s most valuable information.

Yet these environments are often managed separately, with different teams, tools, workflows, and severity models. Attackers do not see those boundaries. They see a single attack surface.

That is why the Risk Operations Center matters.

The Risk Operations Center was never intended to be another dashboard, nor was it intended to replace the SOC. It is an operating model for continuously identifying, prioritizing, validating, and reducing risk across the enterprise before those vulnerabilities can ever be exploited. To fulfill that mission, the ROC must extend beyond traditional IT assets.

As attack surfaces expand and threats accelerate, organizations need more than visibility. They need a way to bring together technology, telemetry, and expertise into a single operating model capable of operationalizing cyber risk management at scale.

That is the vision behind the expanded Global mROC Alliance.

By bringing together the Qualys platform, specialized technology alliance partners, and a global ecosystem of highly trained Risk Operations Center experts, the Global mROC Alliance helps organizations move from identifying risk to systematically reducing it across the enterprise. The goal is not simply to see more risk. It is to help customers outpace increasingly sophisticated threats in the age of AI.

As part of that effort, Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Management (ETM) now integrates telemetry from Lookout and NowSecure for mobile security, and from Claroty and Nozomi Networks for OT, IoT, healthcare, and cyber-physical environments.

This expands visibility into some of the least measured yet most consequential areas of enterprise risk.

More importantly, it creates a common operational model for reducing risk. Qualys ETM and TruRisk provide the visibility to understand exposure, the prioritization to focus on what matters most, and the remediation guidance needed to drive measurable risk reduction across the attack surface.

The objective is not simply broader visibility. The objective is better prioritization and faster risk reduction.

When a vulnerable mobile device, an exposed medical system, an industrial controller, and an internet-facing application are all evaluated through the same framework, security teams can focus on reducing the risks that have the greatest potential impact on the business rather than simply responding to the loudest alerts.

For mobile environments, that means bringing device posture, application risk, operating system vulnerabilities, and threat telemetry into the same risk conversation as cloud, endpoint, and infrastructure exposure. A compromised mobile device with privileged access may represent greater business risk than dozens of lower-priority infrastructure findings.

For healthcare, manufacturing, OT, and cyber-physical environments, it means incorporating risks that have traditionally existed outside mainstream security operations. Through Claroty and Nozomi Networks, organizations gain visibility into environments where operational continuity is paramount and active scanning may not be feasible. Just as importantly, those risks can now be prioritized and managed through the same remediation workflow as the rest of the enterprise. Where patching is not possible, compensating controls such as segmentation and access restrictions become part of the same risk reduction process.

This is the power of Qualys’ Global mROC Alliance.

Technology alliance partners contribute deep visibility into the environments they know best. Qualys ETM and TruRisk transform that telemetry into a common risk language through visibility, prioritization, and remediation. mROC Alliance partners help customers operationalize those insights through advisory services, implementation, managed risk reduction programs, and fully managed Risk Operations Center services.

Together, they provide organizations with a practical path to reducing risk across the entire attack surface, not just the portion that has historically been easiest to measure.

Find out more about the Global mROC Alliance.

Learn More

PHP2Shell is not the story.

PHP2Shell was just the opening act. The real story is that the time between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation continues to shrink while the attack surface continues to expand.

Organizations can no longer afford separate programs for IT, mobile, healthcare, OT, IoT, and cyber-physical risk. They need a common operating model, a common language for prioritization, and a single system for driving remediation.

The organizations that succeed will not be those that discover the most vulnerabilities. They will be those that reduce the most risk in the shortest amount of time.

That is the purpose of the Risk Operations Center.

And that is why the Risk Operations Center is emerging as the operating system for proactive cyber risk reduction in the age of AI.

Full Text:
A single container image that brings Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit to every Kubernetes node, on immutable and mutable Linux alike, deployed the way your container workloads already are.

Key Takeaways

The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image on Docker Hub, bringing host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit to every Kubernetes node without touching the host’s package manager.

It runs as a Kubernetes DaemonSet, so every node that joins the cluster automatically gets an agent. It can be deployed and upgraded through YAML manifests or a unified Helm chart that also deploys Qualys Container Security sensors, for full-stack coverage in a single install.

A single image covers container-optimized operating systems such as AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS, and Red Hat CoreOS, as well as RPM- and Debian-based Linux, including Azure Linux, on both Intel/x64 and ARM.

Policy Audit includes CIS-certified policies for AWS Bottlerocket and Google Container-Optimized OS, and all findings are prioritized with Qualys TruRisk alongside the rest of your estate.

Paired with Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS), it delivers full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane.

The AI Era Is a Container Era

The AI era isn’t arriving on bare metal. It’s arriving on Kubernetes. Model training pipelines, inference services, vector databases, and the agentic workloads that orchestrate them are being built as containers and scheduled across clusters that scale up and down by the minute. The unit of compute is no longer the server. It’s the container, and the node it happens to be running on right now.

That shift changes the math for security teams. The attack surface is no longer a fleet of servers you can enumerate and patch on a monthly cycle. It’s a fleet of nodes that may exist for hours, boot into operating systems that don’t allow you to install a package, and host workloads that move between them without warning. Every one of those nodes is a host, and every host operating system carries its own vulnerabilities and its own configuration risk, regardless of what’s running in the containers above it.

Qualys TotalCloud Kubernetes and Container Security (KCS) extends build-to-runtime coverage for images, containers, and serverless workloads.

The Problem: Host Security Wasn’t Built for Container Platforms

For years, securing a host meant one thing: install an RPM or a DEB on it. That model worked when hosts were long-lived and homogeneous. It breaks down in container platforms in two ways.

Container-optimized operating systems don’t accept packages. AWS Bottlerocket, Google Container-Optimized OS (COS), Red Hat CoreOS, and their peers deliberately lock down the root filesystem and remove the package manager. There’s nothing to yum install. Security tooling has to run the way everything else on these nodes runs: as a container.

Package-based deployment doesn’t fit orchestrated environments. Kubernetes teams manage everything through manifests, Helm charts, and GitOps pipelines. A security agent that has to be installed out of band, node by node, is the one thing on the cluster that isn’t declared, versioned, and reconciled like everything else. It also can’t keep up: a node pool that scales from ten nodes to two hundred during a training run needs security coverage on every node it creates, automatically.

The result is a coverage gap at the foundation. Teams invest in scanning container images and monitoring running containers, and rightly so. But the container runtime, the kubelet, the kernel, and every system library sit on the host OS. If that layer is unmonitored, a clean image running on a vulnerable node is still a vulnerable workload.

The Solution: Qualys Cloud Agent as a Container Image

The Qualys Cloud Agent is now available as a container image, published directly to Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher account. It runs on every node in your cluster as a DaemonSet and delivers the same host-based Vulnerability Management and Policy Audit that the Qualys Cloud Agent provides on any other platform, without touching the host’s package manager.

Qualys Cloud Agent container images on Docker Hub under the verified Qualys publisher.

The image ships with the Qualys Cloud Agent pre-installed and dynamically pulls down the components it needs at runtime, such as application manifests and supporting utilities, so it stays lightweight while remaining fully functional. Because it’s deployed through Kubernetes, the orchestrator does the work your provisioning scripts used to do: every node that joins the cluster gets an agent, and every node that leaves takes its agent with it.

Intel/x64 image: qualys/cloud-agent-container-x64

ARM image: qualys/cloud-agent-container-arm

How Qualys secures the container stack, from the host operating system to running containers and the Kubernetes control plane.

Once you’ve pulled the image, you can download the deployment YAMLs, and a Qualys Helm chart is published on Artifact Hub so the agent can be installed, versioned, and upgraded through the same Helm workflow as the rest of your cluster.

Why It Matters: The Benefits

Combined with TotalCloud KCS, the Containerized Cloud Agent gives you full-stack coverage across the host OS, running containers, and the Kubernetes control plane, for vulnerabilities, audit, and posture, as well as runtime security, drift, and threat detection.

Full Host Coverage for Container-Optimized and Immutable Operating Systems

Immutable operating systems are the right choice for container platforms: a smaller attack surface, atomic updates, and a root filesystem that can’t drift. But immutability cuts both ways. Title: PHP2Shell on Windows and macOS: Automating the PHP Upgrade, With or Without an Agent
Context: PHP has released a critical security update addressing two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (collectively tracked as PHP2Shell), that allow unauthenticated...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) allows unauthenticated remote code execution on exposed PHP servers. PHP has released fixed versions. On Linux, distribution packages carry the fix. On Windows and macOS, they don’t: Microsoft and Apple don’t ship PHP, so the fix is an in-place PHP upgrade that has traditionally been done by hand, one server at a time. Qualys TruRisk Eliminate’s Custom Assessment and Remediation (CAR) capability runs Qualys TRU-published scripts that upgrade each PHP installation to the latest patch release of its current minor series. On Windows, the script verifies the official build by SHA256 and rolls back on failure. On macOS, it upgrades through Homebrew. If a host is on an end-of-life series, the script stops, reports it, and then you apply the PHP2Shell mitigation script instead. The same script runs through the Cloud Agent or, on hosts without one, through an authenticated Qualys scanner. Agentless runs need a Windows or SSH credential with rights to stop services and replace PHP binaries. Plan a maintenance window for both because IIS, Apache, or php-fpm restarts during the upgrade.

PHP has released a critical security update addressing two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (collectively tracked as PHP2Shell), that allow unauthenticated remote code execution against exposed PHP servers.

On Linux, patching is straightforward: distribution vendors ship updated packages, and Qualys TruRisk Eliminate deploys them.

Windows and macOS are a different story. There is no straightforward vendor patch to deploy, so the fix must be a PHP upgrade, which has traditionally required someone to log in to each server and apply it manually. This blog explains how the Qualys Custom Assessment and Remediation (CAR) capability in Qualys TruRisk Eliminate closes the gap for both deployment models: agent-based and agentless (scanner-based).

Why Patch Management Can’t Deliver the Fix on Windows and macOS

Patching works by deploying the fix that an operating system or software vendor publishes. For PHP on Windows and macOS, that fix does not exist in a deployable form.

Windows: no official installer or updater. Microsoft does not ship PHP, and PHP does not ship an installer or an in-place updater for Windows. The official builds on downloads.php.net are plain ZIP archives published in multiple flavors (Thread Safe / Non-Thread Safe, x64 / x86, and per Visual Studio compiler). Upgrading means picking the right build, stopping IIS or Apache, replacing the binaries in place while preserving php.ini and custom extensions, and restarting services. Third-party stacks such as XAMPP, WampServer, Laragon, Chocolatey and Scoop each add their own layout on top of that.

macOS: Apple no longer ships PHP. PHP was removed from macOS in Monterey (12.0), and Apple software updates do not touch it. php.net publishes only source code, so on modern Macs, PHP most commonly comes from Homebrew (the php formula or a versioned php@8.x formula).

The result is that a PHP server on Windows or macOS will appear vulnerable, with no corresponding patch in the TruRisk Eliminate patch catalog. The vulnerability is real; the remediation path is not a patch.

Custom Assessment and Remediation Closes the Gap with TruRisk Eliminate

TruRisk Eliminate covers four remediation paths: patch, mitigate, isolate, or run a custom script. PHP on Windows and macOS needs the fourth. The CAR capability in TruRisk Eliminate lets you run controlled remediation scripts on your assets from the same platform that detected the exposure. The Qualys Threat Research Unit (TRU) has published PHP upgrade scripts for Windows and macOS in the CAR library so that every host is upgraded the same way. Search the library for “PHP Update to Latest Patch Version” under the PHP2Shell category and import the script for each platform.

Figure 1: PHP2Shell category in the CAR script library. Figure 2: The PHP Update to Latest Patch Version script in the CAR script library (PHP2Shell category).

Both scripts are built around the same principles:

Upgrade within the installed minor series only. 8.2.33 moves to the latest 8.2.x, 8.4.27 to the latest 8.4.x. The scripts never jump a major or minor version, so applications keep running on the branch they were tested against.

Mitigate what can’t be upgraded. If the installed series is end-of-life and no longer published, the script stops and reports it instead of guessing. For those hosts, deploy the PHP2Shell mitigation script from the CAR library. It applies configuration changes that block the attack path and restarts the affected services. Mitigation reduces the risk until you can move to a supported branch; it doesn’t replace the upgrade.

Windows: Official Builds, Verified and Rolled Back on Failure

Discovers every PHP installation on the host, not just the one on PATH: machine and per-user PATH entries, common folders (C:\php*, XAMPP, WAMP, Laragon, Program Files, Scoop), IIS FastCGI handlers in applicationHost.config, and any Windows service that launches a PHP binary.

Detects each installation’s exact build flavor (TS/NTS, x64/x86, VC15/VS16/VS17) by querying php.exe itself, then selects the matching official build from downloads.php.net/releases.json.

Honours the machine WinHTTP proxy automatically, since the SYSTEM account has no user proxy settings.

Downloads the archive and verifies its SHA256 against the published hash before anything is touched.

Stops IIS (W3SVC/WAS), Apache and any php/php-cgi processes using that directory, takes a full backup of the PHP folder, copies the new binaries over the top (php.ini and extra extensions are preserved), and confirms the new version by running php.exe.

Rolls back from the backup and restarts services automatically if the post-upgrade version check fails.

macOS: Homebrew Upgrades Within the Same PHP Series

The macOS script handles the realities of Homebrew, as follows:

Confirms PHP is present and resolves the real binary through symlinks into the Homebrew Cellar to determine which formula owns it (php or php@8.x). PHP from MacPorts, MAMP or a manual build is reported and left alone.

Runs brew as the user who owns the Homebrew installation, because Homebrew refuses to run as root even though CAR executes as root. It also repairs any Homebrew files left owned by root from earlier runs so brew can write to them.

Refreshes Homebrew with retry handling for the common “another brew update is already running” case, and falls back to cached formula data if the refresh fails.

Stays on the installed series. If the default PHP formula has moved to a newer series (for example, the host is on 8.2.x but PHP now tracks 8.4), the script installs or upgrades PHP 8.2 and relinks the PHP command to it rather than forcing a major upgrade.

Restarts the php-fpm service via brew services if it was running before the upgrade and prints the final php -v so the result is visible in the job output.

Agent or Agentless: The Same Script Reaches Every Host

When you create a script in CAR, you choose how it reaches the host. Agent Devices run the script locally through the installed Cloud Agent. Perimeter Devices require no Cloud Agent. The script is delivered and executed through an authenticated Qualys scanner. The script content is identical in both cases; only the delivery changes. Select Windows or Mac as the platform to match the script.

Figure 3: Creating the script in CAR. Choose Agent Devices or Perimeter Devices (agentless), then select Windows or Mac as the platform.

Agent-Based Remediation

In ETM, identify Windows and macOS hosts flagged for the PHP2Shell CVEs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) and tag them by platform.

In CAR, create or import the Windows and macOS PHP upgrade scripts with Agent Devices selected and run each against its platform tag.

Schedule the install run in a maintenance window, since IIS, Apache, or php-fpm will be restarted.

Review job results and rescan to confirm the QID closes.

Agentless Remediation

Many exposed PHP servers sit on appliances, DMZ servers, legacy hosts, and systems owned by other teams: a Windows Server in the DMZ running a vendor web application on IIS and PHP, or Mac minis in a build lab owned by engineering. Many can’t run, or aren’t allowed to run, a Cloud Agent.

A network scan can show that these systems are exposed, but remediating them has usually required someone to log in and make changes by hand, one server at a time. With unauthenticated remote code execution on the table, that pace leaves your perimeter open.

With the CAR capability in TruRisk Eliminate, the same Windows and macOS PHP upgrade scripts run directly on scanner-based hosts through the Perimeter Devices option.

Find your scanner-only hosts. In ETM, identify exposed PHP servers using the PHP2Shell CVEs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619).

Create the scripts for Perimeter Devices. In the CAR module of TruRisk Eliminate, select the PHP upgrade script for the host’s platform from the library, choose Perimeter Devices and Windows or Mac, and point it at the scanner appliance that can reach those hosts with the appropriate authentication records (Windows or SSH).

Run the job. Launch the job against your scanner-based hosts. The scripts behave identically whether launched from an agent or a scanner.

Confirm the remediation. Review the job output for the recorded before/after version on each host, then rerun the scan and confirm the QID no longer reports.

What the Job Output Looks Like

Each host returns a short, readable log entry with the execution status and the before/after PHP versions. Below, a scanner-based macOS host is upgraded from PHP 8.2.33 to 8.2.35 within the 8.2 series, with the php@8.2 formula relinked as the active PHP.

Figure 4: CAR job results showing the PHP upgrade output on a scanner-based macOS host.

On Windows, the log additionally lists every PHP installation discovered on the host, the detected build flavor, SHA256 verification, the services stopped and restarted, and the backup folder location.

Figure 5: CAR job results showing the PHP upgrade output on a scanner-based Windows host.

Conclusion

PHP2Shell is a reminder that remediation goes beyond patching. When there is no straightforward vendor patch to deploy, you still need a safe, fast way to close the exposure. With TruRisk Eliminate, you can discover every PHP installation, upgrade it to the latest release of its current series with integrity verification, automatic rollback, and service restart, and do it from the same console that detected the exposure, agentless on scanner-only hosts and through the Cloud Agent where it is installed.

Qualys customers can find the Windows and macOS PHP upgrade scripts, along with the PHP2Shell mitigation script, in the CAR script library. Review the CVEs (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) in ETM and begin with your internet-facing perimeter.

Not a Qualys customer? Access Qualys’ free PHP2Shell mitigation service to help protect your environment against this threat.

Sign Up for Free Mitigation Service

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Will the script jump me from PHP 8.2 to 8.4?

No. It upgrades only within the installed minor series. 8.2.33 moves to the latest 8.2.x. Applications stay on the branch they were tested against.

What happens on an end-of-life series?

The script stops and reports it. Deploy the PHP2Shell mitigation script until you can move to a supported branch.

Does this work without a Cloud Agent?

Yes. Choose Perimeter Devices and run the same script through an authenticated Qualys scanner. You need a Windows or SSH credential with rights to stop services and replace PHP binaries.

What does the Windows script verify?

It detects the build flavor, downloads the matching official build from downloads.php.net, verifies SHA256 before anything is touched, and rolls back from a full backup if the post-upgrade version check fails.

Title: FedRAMP Authorization Is the Easy Part: How to Stay Authorized with Qualys Policy Audit
Context: Its new Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) rules become mandatory for certification on December 7, 2026
Full Text:
Key Takeaways

FedRAMP authorization isn’t the finish line. Providers are expected to keep monitoring their security posture and give federal agencies the information they need for ongoing, risk-based decisions.

CISA’s BOD 26-04, issued on June 10, 2026, moves federal vulnerability management toward risk-based prioritization instead of a single fixed deadline for every finding.

FedRAMP has said the legacy monthly scan is no longer sufficient. Its new Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) rules become mandatory for certification on December 7, 2026.

In PwC’s 2025 Global Compliance Survey, 85% of executives said compliance requirements have grown more complex over the last three years.

Qualys Policy Audit supports a continuous assess, prioritize, remediate, and report workflow. Audit Fix automates remediation, and control mapping lets one validated control count across multiple frameworks.

Ask anyone who has taken a cloud service through the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) what the process feels like, and you’ll hear roughly the same story. Months of control documentation, a System Security Plan running hundreds of pages, a Third-Party Assessment Organization (3PAO) assessment that turns up gaps nobody saw coming, and finally an Authority to Operate (ATO) letter. What that story usually leaves out is that the letter isn’t the finish line. It’s where the real work starts.

Once a Cloud Service Offering is authorized, FedRAMP expects the provider to continue monitoring its security posture and keep feeding federal agencies the information they need to make ongoing, risk-based decisions. On June 10, 2026, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) raised that bar again with Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04, and FedRAMP moved fast to bring its own rules with it.

The takeaway is fairly simple. Getting authorized was never the hard part. Proving, day after day, that your controls are still doing what they’re supposed to do is the hard part, and it’s the problem policy audit automation exists to solve.

Getting FedRAMP authorized is step one. Learn how to stay authorized.

Watch on Demand

Why Point-in-Time Compliance Stopped Working

FedRAMP used to run on a predictable cadence. Assess, authorize, submit monthly scans, repeat. That model has been cracking for a while now, and three things are driving it.

Vulnerability doesn’t just mean a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry anymore. Misconfigurations and control drift are squarely in scope now, so a clean scan can still be hiding a compliance failure.

Environments move faster than assessment cycles do. Cloud-native infrastructure can drift a dozen times a week, while monitoring reports still tend to go out monthly or quarterly.

Regulators have stopped accepting “we’ll catch it at the next audit.” Federal risk management is moving away from calendar-based reviews and toward real-time, exposure-based decisions.

CISA BOD 26-04, in Plain Terms

BOD 26-04, issued by CISA in June 2026, moved federal vulnerability expectations toward continuous, risk-based validation instead of a single fixed deadline applied to every finding. FedRAMP responded within days, confirming that the legacy monthly scan most Rev5 Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) still lean on for their compliance evidence isn’t going to hold up anymore, and setting December 7, 2026, as the date its new Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules become mandatory for certification. For compliance and audit teams, the practical read is simple. The evidence you hand to an assessor has to reflect what’s true right now, not what was true at the last scan.

The Pain Points Teams Keep Naming

Talk to FedRAMP compliance teams, and the same challenges come up again and again:

Finding control gaps before an assessor does, instead of during the assessment window

Keeping configurations from drifting after they were compliant on day one

Prioritizing remediation when continuous assessment produces a continuous stream of findings

Providing continuous visibility instead of handing over a report generated the week before an audit

Producing audit-ready evidence on demand instead of assembling it after the fact

Cutting duplicate effort across overlapping frameworks, since most FedRAMP teams are also carrying National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-53, Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC), Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), and increasingly the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) on the same infrastructure

In PwC’s 2025 Global Compliance Survey of 1,802 executives across 63 territories, 85% said compliance requirements have grown more complex over the last three years, and nearly 90% said the breadth of their compliance responsibilities has expanded over that same period. That pressure adds cost and strains the teams that have to prove compliance. Misconfigurations make it worse: Qualys analysis of more than 1 billion misconfiguration findings shows access control failures account for 38% of exposures, and organizations take an average of 14 months to fix these basic gaps.

None of this is a documentation problem. It’s an automation problem that’s been wearing a documentation costume.

How Policy Audit Solves the Problem

This is where a continuous assess, prioritize, remediate report workflow stops being a slide in a deck and starts being how the work actually gets done.

On the assessment side, instead of a monthly scan, Qualys Policy Audit continuously evaluates technical controls against the FedRAMP baseline, mapping each policy to a technical check, an expected value, and a pass or fail result across every system in scope. That’s the difference between documenting a control on paper and being able to prove it’s still operating the way it was the day you got your ATO.

Qualys lays this out as five practical steps rather than a single feature:

Connect findings to the control context. Connect raw findings to the control and framework context instead of handing teams a pile of technical output to interpret on their own.

Prioritize what impacts audit outcomes. This is where the volume problem gets solved. Research behind the approach found that fewer than 1% of vulnerabilities in a typical environment pose the highest risk or genuinely need immediate action to move audit outcomes, so results get filtered by control criticality, asset scope, internet-facing devices, the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, and risk signals like MITRE ATT&CK mappings, not just counted.

Automate remediation. Remediation is where the old workflow falls apart. Flag a finding, file a ticket, wait, hope someone remembers to re-scan. That process was never fast, and BOD 26-04’s tighter windows make it untenable. Audit Fix closes the loop instead, automating the fix itself and applying it consistently across assets rather than leaving it to a ticket queue.

Map controls across frameworks. A control validated once, whether that’s for FedRAMP, System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2, ISO 27001, General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), or something else, counts toward every other framework it maps to as well, so teams stop re-proving the same control for every audit that comes around.

Shift to continuous audit readiness. Audit outcomes should reflect the current state of the environment, not a snapshot from whenever someone last pulled a report. That’s the same point CISA and FedRAMP are making. For a closer look at each step, read 5 Steps to Turn Compliance Checks into Audit Outcomes.

Qualys Policy Audit doesn’t replace governance, training, or personnel security. Those stay organizational, and a configuration scanner can’t assess them. On the technical side, it assesses your systems against NIST 800-53 controls in families such as:

Configuration management (CM): settings checked against baselines, with drift flagged

System and information integrity (SI): integrity protections and file changes

Audit and accountability (AU): logging and audit settings

Risk assessment (RA): gaps ranked by risk, not just counted

Assessment, authorization, and monitoring (CA): continuous monitoring of control status

That’s not a coincidence. It’s the reason this category of tooling exists in the first place.

The Takeaway

FedRAMP compliance isn’t a project with an end date anymore. It’s an ongoing discipline, and the rules keep tightening. Teams that still treat authorization as the finish line keep getting caught off guard at reassessment. The teams staying ahead of directives like BOD 26-04, rather than scrambling to react to them, are the ones who’ve built assessing, prioritizing, remediating, and reporting into how they run compliance day-to-day, not just how they prepare for an audit.

If you want to see what that looks like, watch our on-demand webinar, “FedRAMP Authorization and What It Now Takes to Keep It.” It features Kaleb Knobel, Senior Security Analyst and Information System Security Officer (ISSO), and Anu Kapil, Director of Product Management. They share how Policy Audit helps organizations continuously assess, prioritize, remediate, and report on FedRAMP readiness, plus what FedRAMP Moderate and High teams should be doing right now.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Why isn’t FedRAMP authorization the finish line?

After authorization, FedRAMP expects providers to keep monitoring their security posture and give agencies the information they need for ongoing, risk-based decisions. Proving that controls still work, day after day, is the harder part.

What is CISA BOD 26-04?

It’s a Binding Operational Directive that CISA issued on June 10, 2026. It prioritizes vulnerability remediation by risk factors such as public exposure, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) status, automatability, and technical impact, instead of applying one fixed deadline to every finding.

How did FedRAMP respond to BOD 26-04?

Within days, FedRAMP said the legacy monthly scanning that most Rev5 services rely on is insufficient. It set December 7, 2026, as the date its new VDR and VER rules become mandatory for certification. Under these rules, providers must evaluate whether each vulnerability is reachable from the internet and likely to be exploited, fix KEVs within BOD 26-04 timelines, and keep responding to vulnerabilities on an ongoing basis.

How does Qualys Policy Audit support FedRAMP compliance?

Policy Audit continuously evaluates technical controls against the FedRAMP baseline. It maps each policy to a technical check, an expected value, and a pass or fail result so that teams can prioritize, remediate, and report on gaps between audits.

Does Policy Audit replace governance or training?

No. Governance, training, and personnel security remain organizational responsibilities. Policy Audit focuses on technical controls.

Key Takeaways

CISA AA26-194A provides actionable guidance to improve the security of Internet-facing Cisco routers against real-world attack techniques.

The advisory focuses on configuration hardening and security hygiene, rather than a single vulnerability or CVE.

Manually validating advisory recommendations across enterprise networks is difficult, time-consuming, and prone to inconsistencies.

Qualys Policy Audit transforms advisory guidance into automated configuration compliance checks, enabling organizations to continuously assess Cisco router configurations.

Organizations can quickly identify configuration gaps, prioritize remediation, and continuously measure compliance using an out-of-the-box assessment policy.

Cybersecurity advisories provide valuable guidance for defending against evolving threats, but their true value lies in how quickly organizations can translate recommendations into measurable security controls. With the release of the CISA Joint Cybersecurity Advisory AA26-194A, security teams now have concrete guidance to strengthen the security posture of their Internet-facing Cisco routers. Title: Waiting on a Node.js Upgrade? Build a Stopgap with the Controls You Own
Context: In the meantime, interim mitigations from the Qualys Threat Research Unit narrow the Brotli, DNS, TLS, and keep-alive attack paths, and WAF, IPS, and EDR protections from major...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Node.js has fixed CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder flaw that can permit remote code execution, in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, but upgrading at scale is slow. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of roughly 3 million Node.js installations have been patched, and 1.7 million run end-of-life lines that will never receive a fix. In the meantime, interim mitigations from the Qualys Threat Research Unit narrow the Brotli, DNS, TLS, and keep-alive attack paths, and WAF, IPS, and EDR protections from major vendors add further layers. Soon, Qualys ETM will factor these controls into risk scores. These controls buy time, but upgrading the runtime remains the only complete fix.

Node.js comes with a clear instruction: upgrade the runtime. The October 21 security release fixes 10 vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder flaw that can permit remote code execution, and three high-severity flaws that weaken DNS and TLS hostname validation. Fixed releases exist for the 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x lines. Upgrading at this scale still takes time, because the vulnerable code lives in the runtime itself, in container images, single-executable applications, and serverless functions that dependency checks never touch. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of the 3.3 million installations have been patched so far, and 1.7 million run end-of-life versions, including 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, and 20.x, that will not receive a fix and must move to a supported line.

Those first days are where mitigations and compensating controls earn their place. They reduce risk while upgrades roll out, and the right visibility shows which runtimes need attention first. Our Node.js blog post covers vulnerabilities, fixed versions, and detection methods.

Here is how to bridge the gap between disclosure and upgrade, in four steps: find and prioritize exposed Node.js, apply interim mitigations, layer the controls you already run, then patch and verify.

Step 1: Find and Prioritize Exposed Node.js

Qualys customers can search for assets affected by CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to see every Node.js runtime across hosts, containers, and cloud workloads. That includes copies that dependency checks miss, such as those in version managers, application folders, and bundled runtimes.

It is important to note that not every vulnerable runtime has the same level of exposure. Start with internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data (CVE-2026-111497), since they are the most direct path to remote code execution. Services that open TLS connections to user-supplied hosts (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483) come next. Runtimes on end-of-life lines need an upgrade plan, as no patches will be available for them. Consider these factors alongside business criticality to decide what to mitigate and upgrade first.

Step 2: Apply Interim Mitigations

Node.js has no official workaround, but the Qualys Threat Research Unit has identified practical interim steps. Each one narrows a specific attack path while you plan the upgrade, and together they complement the fix.

These changes do not eliminate all exploitation paths associated with these CVEs, and some changes may affect application behavior. Therefore, it is crucial to test the affected applications after each change.

Limit Brotli exposure (CVE-2026-111497). Avoid decompressing Brotli from untrusted sources where you can, and cap payload size and decompression ratio at the reverse proxy or WAF.

Use the safer DNS call (CVE-2026-105482). Resolve user-supplied names with dns.lookup instead of dns.resolve*, and reject hostnames that contain NUL characters.

Canonicalize IP addresses (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483, CVE-2026-106072). Convert addresses to canonical form before they reach a TLS connection, and reject fullwidth and other non-canonical forms.

Turn off keep-alive for untrusted servers (CVE-2026-105481). Disable keepAlive on http.Agent for connections to servers you do not control.

Treat the Permission Model as advisory. (CVE-2026-106071, CVE-2026-106073) Do not rely on it as a security boundary on affected versions.

Step 3: Add Layers from the Security Stack You Already Run

The tools already in your environment can work alongside the interim steps, each at a different point in the attack path. Each layer can catch what the one before it misses.

Edge and network: WAF and IPS. WAF and IPS vendors such as Cloudflare, Fortinet, and Check Point have released protections that name the Brotli flaw. They help block exploit requests before those requests reach the Node.js decoder.

After exploitation: EDR. Behavioral and exploit-prevention policies in endpoint tools such as CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and Cortex XDR add a second line of defense. They help stop what an attacker tries next, such as a Node.js process spawning a shell or downloading a binary, and some also act on the memory exploitation itself.

Step 4: Patch, Restart, and Re-Validate

Interim mitigations reduce risk. Upgrading remains the only complete fix. Node.js fixed these flaws in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, while lines such as 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, 20.x, and older receive no fix and must move to a supported release. Customers can deploy supported vendor patches through TruRisk Eliminate, so check the patch catalog for their line. Qualys reports a high patch reliability rating for these updates and no OS reboot requirement for the runtime upgrade.

Confirm That Remediation Is Complete

A patch isn’t finished when the package installs:

Upgrade every copy. Migrate end-of-life lines to a supported release.

Rebuild container images and single-executable applications on the fixed version, then redeploy them.

Restart every service that runs on Node.js. Long-running processes, containers, and single-executable applications keep the vulnerable runtime in memory until they restart.

Rescan and verify. Rescan with Cloud Agent or Container Security and confirm the detection QIDs are closed.

Where to Start

Find. Search for CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to locate every runtime, including copies outside standard install paths.

Prioritize. Put internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data at the top, alongside business criticality.

Mitigate. Apply the Qualys TRU interim steps to runtimes awaiting an upgrade, and test the affected applications.

Layer. Keep applicable WAF, IPS, and EDR protections enabled and current as additional layers, and set the Cloudflare rule to Block.

Patch and verify. Upgrade to a fixed release, rebuild and redeploy what embeds the runtime, restart every Node.js service, and rescan.

Compensating controls buy valuable time, but they do not remove the flaw. Keep tracking every system until it is patched.

The other faces the internet with nothing in front of it. A traditional scan reports them the same way.

Here is how to bridge the gap between disclosure and patch, in four steps: find and prioritize exposed PHP, apply the Qualys mitigation, layer the controls you already run, then patch and verify.

Step 1: Find and Prioritize Exposed PHP

Qualys customers can identify PHP installations through network scans, Cloud Agents, container assessments, and Deep Scan, where supported. Additionally, they can assess exposed web applications and APIs using Qualys TotalAppSec. To facilitate PHP discovery, use QID 45110, followed by the relevant vulnerability-detection QIDs and software-inventory QIDs, to assess the assets in scope.

It is important to note that not every vulnerable host has the same level of exposure. TruConfirm helps validate the indicators of the tested PHP2Shell entry point. Its benign probe checks whether this entry point is reachable and whether the upload-progress mitigation is absent, all without creating files, executing code, or applying memory pressure. For more details, refer to our PHP2Shell blog post, which explains how the probe works.

In one customer environment with 1,539 assets running PHP, TruConfirm returned positive validation results for 25 of those assets. Consider these results alongside their internet exposure and business criticality to determine what vulnerabilities to prioritize for mitigation and patching. Keep in mind that a negative result does not guarantee that all exploitation paths are closed.

Step 2: Apply the Qualys Mitigation

Qualys provides a configuration-level mitigation for PHP2Shell based on PHP’s guidance and insights from the Qualys Threat Research Unit. It turns off session upload progress and hardens related session-handling configuration on supported hosts. This reduces exposure to the confirmed session-lifecycle attack path without requiring application-code changes.

It does not eliminate every exploitation path associated with the two CVEs. Test applications that depend on upload-progress functionality after the change.

With or without an agent. Customers with vulnerable detections can select Mitigate Now from their dashboards. Configuration-level, with restart verification. The mitigation applies configuration changes and automatically restarts the PHP service. Review the execution logs and restart the service manually if a restart is still required. Confirm that every affected PHP worker has picked up the new configuration.

Verified, not assumed. After the restart, Qualys checks the effective configuration to confirm the setting is active and not overridden elsewhere.

Inbound: WAF and IPS. WAF and IPS vendors such as Akamai, Cloudflare, F5, Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, and Check Point have released signatures that name both CVEs.
